config.title: Context Performance

intro.title: Context Performance
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React app that demonstrates how to optimize performance when using React Context. You will learn to prevent unnecessary re-renders by splitting context providers and using memoization techniques like React.memo. The core concept involves understanding how context updates trigger re-renders in consuming components and how to control them. You will work with React's Context API, TypeScript for type safety, and functional components with hooks. By the end, you'll have a practical example showing performance improvements in a controlled scenario.
intro.usecase: React Context performance optimization is crucial in complex applications like e-commerce platforms where product filters, shopping cart states, and user preferences need to be shared across many components. In dashboard applications with multiple real-time data visualizations, poorly optimized context can cause sluggish updates across charts, tables, and status panels. Developers implementing multi-step forms or collaborative editing tools must ensure context updates don't trigger unnecessary re-renders of unrelated UI sections. This pattern is essential for maintaining smooth user interactions in applications with deeply nested component trees that share dynamic state.

objectives: Apply React Context to create a centralized state management solution for components.
Implement the Context.Provider component to wrap and supply state to a component tree.
Utilize the useContext hook to access context values within functional components.
Construct a custom provider component that encapsulates context logic and state management.
Define context types using TypeScript interfaces to ensure type safety across the application.
Use memoization techniques (React.memo) to prevent unnecessary re-renders of child components.
Apply useMemo to compute and cache expensive values derived from context state.
Implement useCallback to memoize callback functions passed through context to child components.
Control component re-renders by splitting context into multiple providers for independent state slices.
Access and modify context state through dedicated functions to maintain predictable state updates.
Compare performance before and after optimization using React DevTools Profiler.
Return optimized component trees that minimize re-renders while maintaining functional requirements.

steps.title: Import React and createContext from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and createContext from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and createContext from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and createContext
import React, { createContext } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and createContext from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an import statement that brings in React and createContext from the 'react' package.
successCriteria: The code must include a valid import statement for React and createContext from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and createContext. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the ability to create context.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both React and createContext from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. Remember to import both React and createContext from 'react'.

steps.title: Import useState and useContext from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import the useState and useContext hooks from the 'react' package. Add the import statement to your existing code.
steps.hint: You need to import two named exports from the same package. Use the import syntax you already know for createContext.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing hooks from 'react'
import { useState, useContext } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: Your code will have both createContext and the two hooks imported from 'react', ready to be used in the component.
successCriteria: The import statement includes both useState and useContext from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported both useState and useContext. These hooks will allow you to manage state and consume context values in your component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but you need to import both useState and useContext from 'react'. Make sure both are included in the same import statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to import both useState and useContext from the 'react' package. The syntax should be similar to how you imported createContext.

steps.title: Create a context with a default value
steps.instruction: Create a context using createContext with an initial value and proper TypeScript interface. Define an interface for the context value and create the context with a default value.
steps.hint: Use createContext to create a context. First define an interface for the context value, then call createContext with a default value that matches that interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed React context with a default value will be created, ready to be used by components.
successCriteria: The code should include: 1) An interface defining the context value type, 2) A call to createContext with a default value that matches the interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a typed React context with a default value. This context will allow components to share state without prop drilling.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be something missing. Make sure you've defined an interface for the context value type and created the context with a default value that matches that interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: The context creation isn't quite right. You need to define an interface for the context value type and then use createContext with a default value that matches that interface.

steps.title: Create a provider component
steps.instruction: Create a functional provider component named 'PerformanceProvider' that accepts children as props. The component should return the context provider with the children wrapped inside.
steps.hint: Define a component that takes 'children' as a prop and returns the context provider wrapping those children.
steps.expectedOutcome: A provider component named 'PerformanceProvider' is created that accepts children and returns the context provider wrapping them.
successCriteria: Returns JSX with context provider wrapping children
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the PerformanceProvider component that will wrap children with the context provider.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your component is named 'PerformanceProvider', accepts children as a prop, and returns the context provider wrapping those children.
steps.feedbackWrong: The provider component isn't quite right. Create a component named 'PerformanceProvider' that takes children as props and returns the context provider with children wrapped inside.

steps.title: Add state to the provider
steps.instruction: Inside your provider component, initialize a state variable called 'isActive' with a boolean default value of false using useState.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to specify the type as boolean.
steps.expectedOutcome: The provider component now has internal state management with an 'isActive' boolean state variable initialized to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added state management to your provider component. The 'isActive' state variable will allow you to track and update a boolean value throughout your context.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've included all required elements: using useState, naming the variable 'isActive', specifying the boolean type, and setting the initial value to false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The provider component doesn't have the correct state setup. Make sure to use the useState hook to create a boolean state variable called 'isActive' with an initial value of false.

steps.title: Create a value object for the context
steps.instruction: Inside your provider component, create a value object that contains the state value and its setter function from useState.
steps.hint: Create a constant named 'value' that's an object with properties for your state value and setter function.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a value object that contains both the state value and its setter function, ready to be passed to the context provider.
successCriteria: The value object must be defined as a constant, include the state value variable, and include the setter function from useState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a value object that contains both the state value and its setter function. This object will be passed to the context provider to make these values available to all child components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your value object includes both the state value and its setter function. Check that you're using the correct variable names from your useState declaration.
steps.feedbackWrong: The value object wasn't created correctly. You need to create an object that contains both the state value and its setter function from useState. Make sure you're using the correct variable names from your useState declaration.

steps.title: Wrap children with the provider
steps.instruction: In the return statement of your MyProvider component, wrap the children with the context Provider component and pass the value object as a prop.
steps.hint: Use the Provider property from your context and pass the value object you created earlier as the value prop.
steps.expectedOutcome: The provider component now properly provides the context value to all its children through the Provider wrapper.
successCriteria: Pass value as a prop to Provider
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wrapped the children with the context Provider, making the context value available to all child components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using MyContext.Provider and passing the value object as a prop.
steps.feedbackWrong: The children need to be wrapped with the context Provider component. Check that you're using MyContext.Provider and passing the value object as a prop.

steps.title: Create a consumer component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named MyConsumer that uses useContext to access the context values from MyContext.
steps.hint: Use the useContext hook with MyContext to get the context value, then return some JSX that displays the count value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new component named MyConsumer that uses useContext to access the context values and returns JSX displaying the count.
successCriteria: Returns JSX that includes the count value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a consumer component that accesses the context values using useContext.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your component uses useContext with MyContext and displays the count value in the returned JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The consumer component needs to use useContext to access the context values and display them in JSX.

steps.title: Display context values in the consumer
steps.instruction: Inside the consumer component, return JSX that displays the count value from the context.
steps.hint: Use the useContext hook to access the context value, then return a paragraph or heading element showing the count.
steps.expectedOutcome: The consumer component should render the count value from the context in the UI.
successCriteria: Uses useContext to get context value
Returns JSX containing the count value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully displayed the context value in the consumer component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to use useContext to access the context and display the count value in the returned JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The consumer component should use useContext to access the context and return JSX showing the count value.

steps.title: Create a button to update context
steps.instruction: Inside the MyConsumer component, add a button element with an onClick handler that calls setCount from the context to increment the count by 1.
steps.hint: You can access setCount from the context value object. Use an arrow function in onClick to call setCount with the current count plus 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MyConsumer component will include a button that, when clicked, increments the count value in the context.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a button that updates the context value when clicked. This demonstrates how to add interactivity to context consumers.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there are some issues. Make sure you're calling setCount with the updated value (count + 1) and that the button has an onClick handler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly set up to update the context. Remember to access setCount from the context and use it in the onClick handler to increment the count.

steps.title: Create a main app component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns JSX containing the MyProvider and MyConsumer components.
steps.hint: Define a component that wraps MyConsumer inside MyProvider. Use the components you've already created.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a main App component that uses the provider and consumer components you've built.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main App component that structures your provider and consumer.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your App component returns JSX that includes MyProvider wrapping MyConsumer.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. Create a component named App that returns JSX with MyProvider and MyConsumer.

steps.title: Render the consumer inside the provider
steps.instruction: In the main App component, return the MyProvider component with MyConsumer as its child.
steps.hint: Wrap the consumer component inside the provider component's JSX tags.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will render the provider wrapping the consumer, establishing the context hierarchy.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wrapped the consumer inside the provider, completing the context setup.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the App component returns the provider with the consumer as a child.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component should return the provider wrapping the consumer. Check your JSX structure.
